courseTitle: Network Security, Endpoint Protection & Threat Detection

lessons.title: Stateful vs. Stateless Firewalls in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: On your own machine, run netstat -ano (Windows) or ss -tnp (Linux) while actively browsing to a couple of HTTPS sites, and identify at least 3 ESTABLISHED connections. For each one, write one sentence explaining what entry you'd expect to find in your OS firewall's state table for that connection (source/dest IP and port, state), and why a reply packet from that same remote server gets let back in automatically without you writing an inbound rule.
slots.deliverable: Real netstat/ss output showing at least 3 ESTABLISHED connections from your own machine, with written notes mapping each one to the state-table entry a stateful firewall would hold for it and why the reply traffic is allowed back in automatically.

lessons.title: Next-Generation Firewalls and Deep Packet Inspection

slots.practicalActivity: Open Wireshark on your lab machine and capture traffic while visiting two completely different HTTPS sites back to back. Both connections use port 443, but inspect the TLS Client Hello for each capture and find the SNI (Server Name Indication) field — the piece of information that, like an NGFW's application-awareness engine, lets something looking at the traffic tell the two services apart even though the port and protocol are identical.
slots.deliverable: Two Wireshark captures of real HTTPS sessions to different sites, each with the TLS Client Hello's SNI field located and labeled, plus a written sentence explaining why a traditional stateful firewall could not make the same distinction a DPI-capable NGFW makes.

lessons.title: DMZ Design and Why Public-Facing Servers Live There

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a network diagram (on paper or any diagramming tool) for a small company that has one public website, an internal file server, and employee workstations, currently all on one flat network. Redesign it with a DMZ holding only the web server, and write one paragraph choosing either a three-legged DMZ or a back-to-back DMZ for this specific company, justifying the choice by cost versus defense-in-depth exactly the way the lesson framed the tradeoff.
slots.deliverable: A real network diagram showing a redesigned DMZ layout for a small company's public web server, plus a written paragraph justifying three-legged vs. back-to-back DMZ for that specific scenario.

lessons.title: VLANs and Network Segmentation Strategy

slots.practicalActivity: Log into your own home router's admin page and check whether it supports a guest Wi-Fi network with device/client isolation enabled (most consumer routers do). If it does, confirm the setting is on and write down exactly what it isolates. Then design on paper a 3-VLAN scheme (Servers / Workstations / Guest Wi-Fi) for a small office, assigning a VLAN ID and subnet to each, and write one sentence per VLAN pair explaining what 802.1Q tagging and a firewall rule would need to block between them.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation (screenshot or written notes) of your home router's real guest-network isolation setting, plus a written 3-VLAN design (IDs, subnets, and the inter-VLAN deny rules needed) for a small office.

lessons.title: IDS vs. IPS: Detection vs. Prevention

slots.practicalActivity: Open your own endpoint protection tool (Windows Defender or equivalent) and find its real-time/behavior-monitoring settings. Identify which features are set to block automatically (IPS-like) versus which only generate a notification/log entry (IDS-like) if your product exposes that distinction. Write a one-paragraph recommendation for a SOC rolling out a brand-new detection rule: should it start in alert-only mode or blocking mode, and why, using the false-positive-as-outage tradeoff from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A written inventory of which of your own endpoint protection's features run in block mode vs. alert-only mode, plus a one-paragraph recommendation on whether a brand-new SOC detection rule should launch in IDS or IPS mode and why.

lessons.title: Signature-Based vs. Anomaly-Based Detection

slots.practicalActivity: Check your own antivirus/endpoint protection's definition-update settings and confirm when it last updated its signature database (most show a timestamp). Then, in your own words, write two short scenarios: one attack a signature-based engine would catch instantly because it's documented, and one novel attack it would completely miss that an anomaly-based baseline engine could still flag — grounding both in real detection categories from the lesson, not invented jargon.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot or note of your own antivirus's real signature-update timestamp, plus two written scenarios distinguishing what a signature-based engine would catch versus what only an anomaly-based engine could catch.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Basic Snort/Suricata Rules

slots.practicalActivity: In a plain text file named rules.rules, hand-write the lesson's SQL injection rule exactly as shown, then write two original rules of your own in the same action/protocol/IP:port -> IP:port/(options) syntax: one that alerts on any TCP traffic to $HOME_NET port 22 containing the string "root login", and one that drops UDP traffic from any source to $HOME_NET port 69 (TFTP). Give each a unique sid starting at 1000002 and a rev, and walk through each field of all three rules out loud in writing.
slots.deliverable: A real rules.rules text file containing the lesson's worked SQL-injection rule plus two original Snort/Suricata-style rules you wrote yourself with unique sids, each with a written field-by-field walkthrough of what it matches and does.

lessons.title: Network-Based vs. Host-Based IDS

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, check whether file integrity monitoring or a HIDS-style agent (Windows Defender's "Controlled Folder Access"/Attack Surface Reduction, or an installed Sysmon/OSSEC agent) is active, and note specifically what local activity it watches. Then write a one-page deployment plan for a small office network: where would you place a NIDS sensor (which link/segment), and which servers would get a HIDS agent, explaining in writing exactly which blind spot each tool covers that the other cannot.
slots.deliverable: Written confirmation of a real HIDS-style capability (file integrity monitoring, ASR, or an installed agent) active on your own machine, plus a written NIDS+HIDS deployment plan for a small office naming specific placement points and the blind spot each covers.

lessons.title: NetFlow and Flow-Based Monitoring

slots.practicalActivity: Run netstat -ano (Windows) or ss -tnp (Linux) on your own machine and pick 5 real active connections. For each one, manually build a flow record exactly as described in the lesson: the 5-tuple (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol) plus an estimated duration and byte count you observe or infer from repeated checks, matching the format of the lesson's worked example.
slots.deliverable: 5 hand-built flow records from your own machine's real active connections, each containing the full 5-tuple plus duration and byte/packet estimates, formatted the way the lesson's concrete NetFlow example was.

lessons.title: Deep Packet Inspection vs. Flow Analysis

slots.practicalActivity: Take one of the 5 flow records you built last session and, for that same connection, capture the real traffic in Wireshark and drill into the payload using the Follow TCP Stream feature to see what the application actually sent. Write a short comparison: what the flow record alone told you versus what the DPI-level Wireshark capture revealed, and explain in writing why you wouldn't run this same deep inspection on all 5 connections continuously.
slots.deliverable: A flow record and a matching Wireshark "Follow TCP Stream" capture of the same real connection, plus a written comparison of what each view reveals and why DPI is reserved for flagged traffic rather than run on everything.

lessons.title: Baselining Normal Traffic to Spot Anomalies

slots.practicalActivity: Over the course of one real day, check netstat/ss or your router's connected-devices page 3–4 times and log your own machine's outbound destinations and rough active hours. At the end of the day, write a one-page personal traffic baseline across the lesson's three dimensions: typical volume, typical destinations (which sites/services you actually talked to), and typical timing (when you were online) — then write one sentence describing what a 3 AM connection to a brand-new destination would look like against that real baseline.
slots.deliverable: A real one-day traffic log of your own machine's connections across volume, destinations, and timing, written up as a personal baseline, plus a written description of what a baseline-breaking anomaly would look like against it.

lessons.title: Detecting Data Exfiltration Patterns in Traffic

slots.practicalActivity: Run nslookup or dig against 5 domains you use regularly and note the query/response pattern, then run the same command against a deliberately long, random-looking subdomain you construct yourself (e.g. a123b456c789d012e345.example.com) to see what an abnormally long DNS tunneling-style query actually looks like on the wire in Wireshark. Write up the 4-signal exfiltration case from the lesson (baseline deviation, beaconing interval, newly registered domain, DNS tunneling under DPI) applied to a fictional host of your own design.
slots.deliverable: Real nslookup/dig output comparing a normal domain query to a deliberately long synthetic one, captured in Wireshark, plus a written exfiltration case for a fictional host walking through all 4 of the lesson's combined signals.

lessons.title: EDR Telemetry: What Gets Collected and Why

slots.practicalActivity: Open Windows Event Viewer on your lab machine and locate a real process-creation event (Event ID 4688 under Security, enabling the audit policy first if needed, or any Sysmon Event ID 1 if Sysmon is installed). Find one real event showing a full command line, parent process, user, and timestamp, and annotate it against the lesson's four telemetry categories (process, network, file, registry), writing one sentence for which category each field belongs to.
slots.deliverable: A real captured Windows process-creation event (4688 or Sysmon Event ID 1) from your own machine showing a full command line and parent process, annotated field-by-field against the lesson's four EDR telemetry categories.

lessons.title: Process Trees and Behavioral Detection

slots.practicalActivity: Open Task Manager's Details tab (or Process Explorer) on your lab machine, open a Word or text document to trigger a real parent-child process launch, and use Process Explorer's tree view (or the parent PID column) to confirm the actual lineage, e.g. explorer.exe -> winword.exe. Document that real, benign chain, then write out the lesson's winword.exe -> powershell.exe -> certutil.exe suspicious chain beside it and explain in writing exactly what makes one noise and the other a high-confidence alert.
slots.deliverable: A real captured process tree from your own machine (via Task Manager Details or Process Explorer) showing an actual parent-child launch, paired with a written comparison against the lesson's winword.exe -> powershell.exe -> certutil.exe example explaining what separates noise from a high-confidence alert.

lessons.title: Detecting Living-off-the-Land Techniques

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM (never a production machine), run certutil -urlcache -split -f against a safe, known URL (e.g. a Microsoft or GitHub raw file) and observe the exact command-line pattern a SOC's EDR would flag. List the 4 LOLBins from the lesson (PowerShell, WMI, certutil, PsExec) and check which ones are present on your own machine by default, then write one sentence per tool explaining what command-line pattern or context would separate your legitimate test run from an attacker's use of the same binary.
slots.deliverable: Real certutil -urlcache output from a safe test download on your lab VM, plus a written audit confirming which of the 4 LOLBins exist on your own machine and the specific command-line/context signal that would distinguish legitimate use from attacker use for each.

lessons.title: EDR Response Actions: Isolation and Containment

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, disable just the network adapter (Disable-NetAdapter in PowerShell or ifconfig down on Linux) while leaving the machine running, and confirm with a ping test from another machine that it's unreachable while still fully operational locally — this is the real mechanic behind EDR host isolation. Then write a comparison explaining specifically what evidence (running processes, injected code, connection state) a full shutdown would have destroyed that staying powered on and isolated preserved.
slots.deliverable: Proof (screenshots/commands) of disabling a lab VM's network adapter while keeping it running and confirming unreachability, plus a written explanation of what forensic evidence a full power-off would have destroyed that isolation preserved.

lessons.title: What an IOC Actually Is and Common Types

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the real SHA256 hash of any file on your machine using certutil -hashfile <path> SHA256 (Windows) or sha256sum <path> (Linux/Mac). Make a copy of that file, rename it, and move it to a different folder, then hash the renamed copy and confirm the hash is byte-for-byte identical — proving in practice why a file hash survives renaming as a reliable IOC. Write one example each of the lesson's other 3 IOC types (malicious domain, registry key, email pattern) in your own words.
slots.deliverable: Two real SHA256 hash outputs — the original file and a renamed, relocated copy of it — proven identical, plus 3 written example IOCs covering malicious domain, registry key, and email-pattern types.

lessons.title: Threat Intelligence Feeds and How SOCs Use Them

slots.practicalActivity: Research and name one real example of each of the lesson's 3 feed sources: a commercial threat-intel vendor, a real ISAC (e.g. the FS-ISAC for finance or H-ISAC for healthcare), and a real free open-source feed project (e.g. abuse.ch or AlienVault OTX). Visit the open-source one directly and find a real, currently-listed malicious IP or domain on its site. Write a short paragraph describing how a TIP would ingest that specific indicator and push it to a firewall automatically.
slots.deliverable: Named real examples of a commercial vendor, an ISAC, and an open-source threat-intel feed, with one real currently-listed IOC pulled directly from the open-source feed's site, plus a written description of the automatic TIP-to-firewall enforcement loop.

lessons.title: STIX and TAXII: Sharing Threat Intelligence

slots.practicalActivity: Look up a real, published STIX bundle example (OASIS's own STIX 2.1 documentation or MITRE's examples both publish sample JSON) and identify the object types used (indicator, malware, threat-actor, relationship). Then hand-write your own small STIX-style JSON object describing a fictitious malicious IP indicator, following the same field structure you observed, and write one paragraph explaining why that data needs TAXII as a separate transport layer rather than being bundled into one combined standard.
slots.deliverable: Notes from a real published STIX bundle example identifying its object types, plus your own hand-written STIX-style JSON indicator object and a written explanation of why STIX and TAXII are kept as separate standards.

lessons.title: Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) for Defenders

slots.practicalActivity: Run a real WHOIS lookup (whois command or any public WHOIS web tool) against a domain you own or a well-known public domain, and record the registrar and registration date it returns. Run a real search on Shodan.io (free account) for your own current public IP address and note what it shows is exposed. Check one of your own email addresses against haveibeenpwned.com and record the real result. Write a one-paragraph summary of what a defender would do differently than an attacker running the exact same three searches.
slots.deliverable: Real WHOIS, Shodan, and Have I Been Pwned results for your own domain, IP, and email respectively, plus a written paragraph on what distinguishes a defender's use of those exact same tools from an attacker's.

lessons.title: Vulnerability Scanners: Nessus and OpenVAS Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: Install Nessus Essentials (free, scans up to 16 IPs) or OpenVAS/Greenbone Community Edition in your lab VM, and run one real scan against your own lab machine or a deliberately vulnerable VM (e.g. Metasploitable) that you control — never a network you don't own. Capture the real findings list it produces, and for one finding, trace it back to the specific plugin/NVT and CVE it matched.
slots.deliverable: A real Nessus Essentials or OpenVAS scan run against your own lab VM, with the findings report captured and one specific finding traced back to its plugin/NVT ID and CVE.

lessons.title: Authenticated vs. Unauthenticated Scans

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same scanner from last session, run an unauthenticated scan against your own lab VM, then configure and run an authenticated scan against that same VM using a real local admin/SSH account you control. Compare the two findings counts and write up at least 2 specific findings the authenticated scan caught that the unauthenticated scan structurally could not have seen, citing the real difference in what each scan mode had access to.
slots.deliverable: Two real scan reports — unauthenticated and authenticated — run against the same lab VM, with a written comparison naming at least 2 findings only the authenticated scan could have caught and why.

lessons.title: Reading a Vulnerability Scan Report

slots.practicalActivity: Take the real scan report from your last two sessions (or a sample Nessus/OpenVAS report found via a vendor's published example) and pick 3 findings. For each, write out its full anatomy (host, CVE, severity, description, remediation) in your own table, then rank all 3 by the lesson's real 3-factor prioritization (severity, exploitability, asset criticality) rather than by raw CVSS score alone, explaining your ranking in writing.
slots.deliverable: A written table of 3 real scan findings with full anatomy (host/CVE/severity/description/remediation), re-ranked by severity + exploitability + asset criticality with a written justification for the final order.

lessons.title: Scan Scheduling and the Vulnerability Management Lifecycle

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real finding from your earlier scan reports, apply an actual remediation (install a missing update, change a flagged configuration setting) on your lab VM, then rescan and confirm in the new report that the finding no longer appears — the real verify step from the lifecycle. Write a scan-scheduling policy for a fictional small company with 3 asset tiers (internet-facing, internal servers, internal workstations), assigning a different real cadence to each and justifying it by exposure and value.
slots.deliverable: A before/after scan report pair from your own lab VM proving a real remediation and verify step closed a finding, plus a written 3-tier scan-scheduling policy with justified cadences for each tier.

lessons.title: What a Honeypot Actually Is and Why It Works

slots.practicalActivity: On a lab VM with no production data or users, start a simple listener on an unused port with no legitimate purpose (e.g. nc -lvp 2222 on Linux or a PowerShell TCP listener on Windows) and leave it running for a while, checking back for any connection attempts — a minimal, hand-built honeypot. Write up the lesson's 3 real jobs a honeypot does (early warning, studying behavior, slowing attackers) and explain, specific to your own listener, why any single connection to it would be inherently suspicious.
slots.deliverable: A real listener running on an unused port on your lab VM with logged results (even if no hits occurred), plus written notes applying the lesson's 3 honeypot functions and explaining why any interaction with your listener would be inherently suspicious.

lessons.title: Low-Interaction vs. High-Interaction Honeypots

slots.practicalActivity: Install Cowrie (a real, free low-interaction SSH/Telnet honeypot) in an isolated lab VM with no path to any other network, following its real setup docs, and confirm it's logging simulated login attempts you make against it yourself. Write a comparison explaining why Cowrie counts as low-interaction (no real shell behind it) versus what a high-interaction equivalent would require, and the extra isolation precaution a high-interaction honeypot demands that your low-interaction one does not.
slots.deliverable: A real Cowrie honeypot installed and running in an isolated lab VM, with logged login attempts captured, plus a written comparison of low- vs. high-interaction honeypots and the isolation precautions each requires.

lessons.title: Deception Technology Beyond the Honeypot

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, plant a real honeytoken: create a text file named aws-credentials.txt containing a fake, clearly non-functional AWS access key, and create an empty decoy folder named something tempting like IT-Admin-Passwords. Write a one-page deception plan for a small company extending these two tripwires with a fake AD service account name, and explain in writing why spreading several of these cheap decoys catches more lateral movement than relying on one honeypot alone.
slots.deliverable: A real honeytoken file and decoy folder created on your lab VM, plus a written deception plan adding a fake AD object and explaining why spreading multiple cheap decoys beats relying on a single honeypot.

lessons.title: Why Honeypot Alerts Are High-Fidelity Signals

slots.practicalActivity: Review the real logs from your Cowrie honeypot and your listener/honeytoken from the previous 3 sessions. Write a short comparison memo: how many total "hits" you logged across all your deception assets versus how many real alerts a typical firewall or antivirus generates on your own machine in a single day (check your own security software's alert/log history for a real count), and explain in writing why your honeypot's much smaller number of alerts is more trustworthy than the much larger number of firewall/AV alerts.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison memo citing your own real honeypot/honeytoken hit count against your own machine's real firewall/antivirus alert count over the same period, explaining why the smaller honeypot number carries higher confidence.

lessons.title: Lab: Designing a Segmented Network with a DMZ
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Layered Threat Detection Program

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the Castellan Retail lab exactly as the lesson lays it out: draw the 3-interface perimeter firewall (WAN/DMZ/Internal), place the web server alone in the DMZ, and write out all 4 firewall rules from the lesson (WAN->DMZ allow/deny, DMZ->Internal host-to-host allow/deny) in a real rule-table format. Then extend the lab yourself by adding a 4th VLAN of your own choosing (e.g. a VoIP or IoT segment) and writing the rule that isolates it from VLANs 10 and 20 the same way Guest Wi-Fi was isolated.
slots.deliverable: A completed network diagram and full firewall rule table for the Castellan Retail DMZ/VLAN lab, plus a written 4th VLAN addition of your own with its own isolation rule, following the lesson's exact rule-scoping pattern.

lessons.title: Lab: Writing Detection Rules for a Known Attack Pattern
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Layered Threat Detection Program

slots.practicalActivity: In a real rules file, hand-write both of the lesson's two Suricata rules exactly as shown — the sqlmap User-Agent rule and the beaconing dsize/threshold rule — with correct sids. Then write a third original rule of your own for a different known attack pattern (e.g. detecting a Nikto web-scanner's default User-Agent, using the same http.user_agent sticky-buffer technique), and write one paragraph on how you'd tune it to avoid a false positive, following the lesson's own tuning example.
slots.deliverable: A real rules file containing both of the lesson's worked Suricata rules plus one original rule you wrote for a different known attack pattern using the same sticky-buffer technique, with a written tuning note addressing a realistic false positive.

lessons.title: Case Study: Catching a Slow Data Exfiltration
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Layered Threat Detection Program

slots.practicalActivity: Write a full incident report for the Castellan Retail exfiltration case exactly as the lesson presents it: name all 3 signals (NetFlow baseline deviation, threat-intel-flagged destination, EDR process telemetry/masquerading svch0st.exe), draw the real process tree from the lesson, and write the containment response in the order it actually happened. Then write one paragraph identifying which single signal, if it alone had been missing, would have let this exfiltration go undetected the longest, and why.
slots.deliverable: A written incident report reconstructing the Castellan exfiltration case's 3 signals, process tree, and containment sequence, plus a written analysis of which single signal was most load-bearing for catching it.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: Network Security & Threat Detection Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Layered Threat Detection Program

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph summary of each of the course's 8 chapters in your own words, explicitly naming which layer (prevention, detection, or response) each one belongs to, the same way the lesson's recap does. Then write your own resume bullet naming the specific tools and techniques you actually used across this course's labs (Suricata rules, DMZ/VLAN design, Nessus/OpenVAS or Cowrie if you ran them, WHOIS/Shodan), and a short portfolio README summarizing the Castellan Retail capstone work across Lessons 29–31.
slots.deliverable: A written 8-chapter course recap naming each chapter's prevention/detection/response layer, plus a written resume bullet and portfolio README summarizing the specific real tools and labs used across the Castellan Retail capstone.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can design a segmented network with a properly scoped DMZ and host-to-host firewall rules, explain and configure the real tradeoffs between stateful/stateless firewalls and NGFW deep packet inspection, read and hand-write working Snort/Suricata detection rules (including sticky buffers, dsize, and threshold tuning), and tell network-based from host-based detection apart by what each one structurally can and cannot see. They can build a real traffic baseline from flow data and recognize the specific signature of data exfiltration — low-and-slow transfers, beaconing intervals, and DNS tunneling — and they can read raw EDR telemetry (process creation, network, file, registry, DLL loads), build and interpret a process tree, and recognize living-off-the-land abuse of tools like PowerShell, WMI, certutil, and PsExec. They know how to isolate a compromised host without destroying volatile-memory evidence, work with real IOCs and threat intelligence feeds (including STIX/TAXII sharing and OSINT tools like WHOIS and Shodan), run and interpret authenticated and unauthenticated vulnerability scans through the full scan-prioritize-remediate-verify lifecycle, and deploy honeypots and honeytokens as deliberately high-fidelity tripwires. Having worked the Castellan Retail capstone end to end, they've combined flow analysis, threat intel, and EDR telemetry into one real multi-signal detection case — the same layered reasoning a SOC analyst applies daily, now ready to carry into the next course's SOC operations and SIEM work.
